title: Logical replication primary-key conflict after pg_createsubscriber under heavy load
body: I am converting PostgreSQL 17.4 databases on RHEL 9 from pglogical to native logical replication. In rare cases, after converting a physical replica with pg_createsubscriber while the primary remains live and under load, the logical replica starts with replication stuck on a conflicting primary key even though the replica received no client connections and only received changes from that primary. I have a shell script that repeatedly creates a primary and physical replica, generates concurrent inserts, converts the replica to logical replication, and compares row counts. Reproduction can take minutes or hours; NUM_THREADS=40 and INSERT_WIDTH=1000 is a useful starting point on a powerful machine. The script was pasted into the report and then supplied again because email formatting may have damaged it.

symptoms_visible: In rare runs after converting the physical replica with pg_createsubscriber, logical replication stops on a conflicting primary key.
The replica received no client connections and only received changes originating from the one live primary.
N0.label: N0 intermittent replication conflict reported

symptoms_visible: The logical replication apply worker repeatedly exits with a duplicate-key violation for a primary-key value that is already present on the converted replica.
This is not just a decoder process taking time to catch up.
N1.label: N1 apply-worker conflict confirmed

symptoms_visible: Even after allowing more time for synchronization, the apply worker remains unable to proceed because the same insert encounters an existing primary-key value.
N2_x.label: N2_x waiting-for-catchup aftermath

symptoms_visible: The converted replica still contains the row before logical replication tries to insert that same primary-key value again.
N3.label: N3 duplicate replay mechanism established

symptoms_visible: A maintainer reports that the fix has been pushed, but I have not retested a build containing it on my own system.
N_terminal.label: terminal fix pushed without reporter retest

question_patterns: Can you share the exact replication error and identify which PostgreSQL process is stopping?
How did you distinguish a permanent conflict from the subscriber merely taking time to catch up?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I confirmed from the replica log that the logical replication apply worker is exiting on a duplicate-key violation because the primary-key value already exists. It remains stuck on that conflict rather than simply catching up.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: There is no duplicate-key error; the row counts become equal once I wait for the subscription to synchronize.
The duplicate-key error names a different key value on each reproduction, but it is always the logical replication apply worker that exits.

edges.comment: Reporter messages c4-c5: Zane rejects the suggestion that the test merely stopped too early, says the process is stuck on a primary-key conflict, and corrects 'decoder process' to 'logical apply worker'. This edge describes the reporter's own system.

solution.intent: Treat the row-count mismatch as ordinary replication lag and wait for subscription synchronization before comparing the databases.
solution.concrete_example: Replace the fixed sleep with wait_for_subscription_sync, or increase the sleep interval, and only compare row counts after the subscriber catches up.

edges.comment: Participant4 c3 suggested that the script might only be observing lag and recommended waiting for synchronization. Reporter c4-c5 supplied contrary evidence from his own system: the apply worker was persistently exiting on a duplicate-key conflict, so additional waiting did not address the failure.

solution.intent: Diagnose the conflict as the same transaction being applied once during physical recovery and then emitted again by logical decoding when the consistent LSN points to the start of a COMMIT record.
solution.concrete_example: Inspect WAL around the slot's confirmed-flush position: it can be the end of a RUNNING_XACT record and therefore the start of the following COMMIT record. Inclusive recovery applies that COMMIT before promotion, while logical decoding later sends the same transaction to the subscriber.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied the stress scenario and duplicate-key behavior. Contributors c6-c8 and c17-c23 derived the WAL-boundary mechanism: confirmed_flush_lsn can be the end of RUNNING_XACT and thus the starting address of a following COMMIT; inclusive recovery applies that record, and logical decoding emits its transaction again. The warning that simply advancing to the next WAL record could lose data is also engineer analysis.

edges.comment: Engineering analysis from c6-c8 and the final accepted refinement in c17-c23. Participant3 and other PostgreSQL contributors reproduced the reporter's scenario on separate test systems; their WAL inspection is engineer-side inference, not presented as output produced by the reporter.

solution.intent: Change pg_createsubscriber's recovery setup so recovery stops before the record at the consistent LSN, preventing that transaction from being applied physically before logical replication starts, and ask the reporter to verify a build containing the fix.
solution.concrete_example: Generate recovery configuration with recovery_target_inclusive=false for pg_createsubscriber. This stops recovery immediately before the WAL record beginning at the consistent LSN, allowing logical replication to apply it exactly once. Maintainer stress tests ran for several hours without reproducing the conflict, and the fix was pushed; the original reporter should still retest a build containing the change.

edges.comment: Final accepted fix from c10-c24: the earlier idea of advancing the replication origin to the next WAL record was replaced because it could skip required data. Contributors tested the revised patch on separate systems, and participant2 reported that it was pushed. The reporter did not confirm the landed fix on his own system, so the terminal state remains unverified.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted root cause: the slot's consistent LSN can be the start address of a COMMIT record, and inclusive recovery applies that transaction physically before logical decoding sends it again, causing the duplicate-key conflict.
Diagnosis must be grounded in the reporter's apply-worker duplicate-key evidence and the WAL-boundary analysis, rather than treating the row-count mismatch as ordinary replication lag.
Must not recommend merely waiting longer or only using subscription synchronization as the fix; the apply worker was persistently failing on an existing primary key.
Must not solve the issue by blindly advancing to the next WAL record, because the thread identified a risk of skipping data.
The accepted technical fix must stop recovery before the record at the consistent LSN by making the recovery target non-inclusive.
Must ask the affected reporter to verify a build containing the fix and must not claim user-verified resolution, because only maintainers tested the patch and reported that it was pushed.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced PostgreSQL operator and automation author who manages physical and logical replication, can build repeatable shell stress tests, inspect server logs, and distinguish decoder, walsender, and apply-worker behavior.
persona_hint.communication_style: Technical, precise, and cooperative; provides reproducible workload details, corrects terminology when needed, and challenges alternative explanations with direct log evidence.
